question.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ -15 & -5\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=1-3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}.$

Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14133513/assets/968084db2423806f55db98d47b3d990ee4947c78bf9f47e0148233dacea68dc3.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14133513/assets/5a9654d8ba7c344ef4b4690f3ba76863a7b156160ac788dca629940b36f69b6e.svg) be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14133513/assets/da4cabb68fce3b6e8d514bed9cd3a14c56d5428ecbd2060e10f4711b7cb0b0cf.svg)
Given that $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of ${\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}}.$
current_example.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =4+5\textrm{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5\text{i}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}-5\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(4+5\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = \textrm{i}x_1.
$$

So, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14133513/assets/da5290e2a5e96efc7c44316f8fef746f9c6dfa7b0065cf3cede7b9fc47fce8f9.svg)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14133513/assets/a2befac7bdffb5276eca49e4b9da5e8839aba3ef445deee2f84894db77652e87.svg) 

Now, since $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda_1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\lambda_2=\overline{\lambda_1}=4-5\textrm{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf v_1.$ Therefore, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14133513/assets/48a625c482b5fd6dca4f00532e321913ec63c7b7f791ff8869cdfd2dd79f5cdf.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
{\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}} = {\dfrac{(1)(1)}{(\textrm{i})(-\textrm{i})}} = 1.
$$
